articles.title: Sky Brown: GB skateboarder wins silver at World Skate Games
articles.summary: Great Britain's youngest Olympic medal winner, Sky Brown, wins silver at the World Skate Games in Paraguay, helping her LA 2028 qualifying hopes.
articles.body:
Great Britain's Sky Brown won silver at the World Skate Games as she continued her bid to qualify for a third Olympic Games.

The 18-year-old skateboarder scored 89.50 points in the women's park final and narrowly missed out on gold to Japan's Mizuho Hasegawa, who scored 91.00.

The competition in Asuncion, Paraguay, was the second event where skaters could earn world skate ranking (WSR) points towards qualifying for Los Angeles 2028, which will be the third Olympic Games to host skateboarding.

In the Tokyo Olympic Games, held in 2021, Brown won bronze to become Great Britain's youngest Olympic medal winner at 13 years old.

Four years later, she added a second bronze at the Paris Olympics.

Brown is also a two-time park world champion, winning titles in 2023 and 2025.

Her 15-year-old brother, Ocean Brown, also competed for Great Britain in Paraguay, in his first appearance at the World Skate Games, but missed out on advancing past the heats.

articles.title: 'India-Pakistan flavour will be missed': Suraj Karkera on rivals' withdrawal from Asian Champions Trophy
articles.summary: The absence of an India-Pakistan clash may take away some of the intensity and excitement from the upcoming Asian Champions Trophy (ACT) Punjab 2026, but
articles.body: The absence of an India-Pakistan clash may take away some of the intensity and excitement from the upcoming Asian Champions Trophy (ACT) Punjab 2026, but defending champions India remain focused on retaining their title, goalkeeper Suraj Karkera has said. With Pakistan withdrawing from the continental tournament and Bangladesh stepping in as their replacement, the Indian team will turn its attention towards continuing its dominance in Asian hockey.Pakistan's withdrawal leaves India-Pakistan rivalry on the sidelinesPakistan's withdrawal has ruled out a potential India-Pakistan showdown at the Asian Champions Trophy, scheduled to be held from October 27 to November 5 across Jalandhar and Mohali in Punjab.Bangladesh have replaced Pakistan in the six-team tournament after the Pakistan Hockey Federation's participation remained subject to government clearance. PHF president Mohyuddin Ahmed Wani had earlier indicated that the federation would follow the government's decision regarding the team's proposed visit to India.India and Pakistan share one of the most intense rivalries in international hockey, with their encounters traditionally drawing considerable attention from fans. However, the recent head-to-head record has heavily favoured India.In their last 20 meetings since 2016, India have won 18 matches, while the remaining two ended in draws. Pakistan are yet to register a victory during that period. Their most recent encounter came in the semifinal of the 2026 Asian Games, where India edged Pakistan 4-3.'India-Pakistan flavour will be missed' - KarkeraKarkera acknowledged that fans would miss the fierce rivalry between the two neighbours, but stressed that players have little control over decisions surrounding participation in international tournaments. The Indian team, he added, would concentrate on performing to the best of its ability.“They are a good team, and athletes never want to pull out of a tournament, but these are things beyond our control. We're just there to go and perform to the best of our ability, and I think the result will take care of itself. The India-Pakistan flavour will be missed by the people, but it is something that is way beyond our say,” Karkera told ANI.The Indian goalkeeper was speaking on the sidelines of a felicitation ceremony where Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth interacted with and felicitated Indian Army sportspersons who participated in the 2026 Asian Games.India aim to defend Asian Champions Trophy titleWith Pakistan out of the tournament, the competition will feature India, Malaysia, Japan, South Korea, China and Bangladesh. India will enter as defending champions, reigning Asian Games gold medallists and the highest-ranked team in the field.The Indian men's hockey team arrives in Punjab on the back of another successful Asian Games campaign in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, where it successfully defended its gold medal with a commanding 5-1 victory over Malaysia in the final.The triumph marked India's fifth men's hockey gold at the Asian Games, following their victories in 1966, 1998, 2014 and 2022. It also marked a historic edition for Indian hockey, as both the men's and women's teams won gold medals at the same Asian Games for the first time.India, five-time winners of the Asian Champions Trophy, will now look to carry that momentum into the continental competition and strengthen their position among Asia's leading hockey nations.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 2036 Olympics: How South Korea, Qatar, Munich, South Africa, Türkiye, Hungary compare with Ahmedabad's bid
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has confirmed seven interested parties for the 2036 Summer Olympics: India, Germany, Qatar, South
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has confirmed seven interested parties for the 2036 Summer Olympics: India, Germany, Qatar, South Korea, South Africa, Türkiye and Hungary. With the process currently at the dialogue stage, the bids will be shortlisted in March 2027, preferred hosts will be identified in December 2028, and the host will be announced in mid-2029.Germany's candidate is Munich; South Korea's project is associated with Jeonju and Jeonbuk, as well as Seoul; Qatar's is centred on Doha; and South Africa is considering a multi-city or nationwide model. Hungary has designated Budapest as its central venue, while Türkiye is planning to host the 2036 Summer Olympics in Istanbul and India in Ahmedabad.South KoreaSouth Korea is no stranger to hosting the Olympics. Seoul hosted the 1988 Summer Olympics, a landmark event in the country's emergence on the international stage. PyeongChang hosted the 2018 Winter Olympics, giving the country experience of hosting both the Summer and Winter Games.What is South Korea's 2036 project?The domestic selection process produced a significant change in direction. The Korean Sport & Olympic Committee selected Jeonbuk (North Jeolla Province), with Jeonju as its focal city, as the country's domestic candidate. The wider discussion has also involved Seoul, which has its own infrastructure and Olympic legacy.Jeonbuk has been pushing an Olympic plan that uses venues across the province and other Korean cities, while Seoul's supporters have argued that its existing facilities and transport infrastructure make it a more credible option.The regional approach could distribute the benefits of the Games beyond the capital. It also raises a practical question: how will the country present a single, coherent proposal to the IOC when different domestic stakeholders have championed different hosting models?What should Ahmedabad learn from South Korea?South Korea's advantage is its proven experience in delivering the Olympics. Ahmedabad, by contrast, is building its case around the 2030 Commonwealth Games and the possibility of using the Olympics to transform India's sporting ecosystem.The comparison, therefore, is not simply about how many stadiums each city has. It is about whether Ahmedabad can offer the IOC an equally convincing account of how the venues will work, how athletes will move between them, and what will remain after the Games.QatarQatar is selling accumulated investment and operational readiness. Rather than making the Olympics the starting point for a major infrastructure build-out, it wants to demonstrate that much of the necessary infrastructure is already in place.Doha previously sought to host the Summer Olympics in 2016 and 2020 but failed to reach the final stage of either selection process. The 2016 project was rejected at the applicant stage, while the 2020 campaign did not make the final group of candidate cities.Since then, Qatar has substantially expanded its major-event credentials. Its record includes:- The 2022 FIFA World Cup.- The 2023 AFC Asian Cup.- The 2024 World Aquatics Championships.- The 2030 Asian Games, which Qatar is scheduled to host.This record gives Qatar something that a first-time Olympic host cannot easily replicate: experience in managing a major-event ecosystem, including stadiums, accommodation, transport, broadcasting and international sporting operations.What is Qatar's 2036 project?Qatar's pitch is centred on Doha and the wider metropolitan area, with Lusail and Al Rayyan among the locations relevant to its existing sports infrastructure.The Qatar Olympic Committee has said that approximately 95% of the required sports infrastructure is already available. The final project will still need to establish the suitability of venues, their capacity, operating arrangements and any gaps that must be addressed.Its approach is tied to Qatar National Vision 2030, with an emphasis on sustainability, inclusion, legacy and limiting unnecessary construction. The country is also looking to build on the facilities and experience developed for the 2022 World Cup.One important complication is the calendar. Doha's summer temperatures could make a conventional July-August Olympics difficult. Qatar's 2022 World Cup was moved to November and December because of the heat, and a Summer Olympics in Qatar would face a comparable question about competition conditions and scheduling.What should Ahmedabad learn from Qatar?Qatar sets the benchmark for infrastructure readiness and delivery experience. Its challenge is not whether it can build major sports facilities, but whether it can make the case for a Summer Olympics that meets athletes' needs, accounts for the climate and delivers an enduring public legacy.Ahmedabad can counter with a different argument: hosting would accelerate the development of a sports ecosystem in a country with a vast population and a large potential athlete base. However, the Indian proposal will need to be precise about which facilities already exist, which are planned and how each investment will be used after 2036.Qatar's experience also offers a warning for India: successfully delivering one mega-event does not, by itself, settle questions about long-term legacy, sustainability or international scrutiny.Munich, GermanyMunich, which hosted the 1972 Games, wants to show that a modern Olympics need not be a giant construction project. Its proposition centres on existing venues, short distances, a familiar Olympic setting and the conversion of Games infrastructure into long-term public assets.The year 2036 has particular significance: it would fall exactly 100 years after the Berlin Games, which the Nazi regime exploited for propaganda. This gives Germany an opportunity to frame the event around democratic values and a very different modern identity, but it also makes the anniversary politically sensitive.Germany's domestic selection process was competitive. Munich defeated Cologne-Rhine-Ruhr in the German Olympic Sports Confederation's selection, winning by 90 votes to 51. Hamburg's earlier plans had been rejected in a referendum, while Berlin withdrew its proposal. Munich was eventually selected as Germany's candidate for the 2036, 2040 or 2044 Games.What is Munich's 2036 project?The German Olympic Sports Confederation's official concept, Munich for Germany, has several distinguishing features:- Existing facilities: The Olympic Park, which hosted events in 1972, is the centrepiece.- Short distances: Munich wants to keep a large proportion of competition venues within a compact geographical area.- A recognisable city setting: Locations such as the English Garden, Nymphenburg Palace and Odeonsplatz feature in the wider vision.- Post-Games housing: The Olympic and Paralympic Village is intended to become a climate-neutral, accessible neighbourhood for more than 10,000 people.- Sustainability: The bid promotes the circular use of resources and a legacy that extends beyond the event itself.The DOSB says approximately half of all competitions would take place in the Olympic Park. The concept is intended to reduce the need for new construction and make use of Munich's existing sporting infrastructure.Munich's domestic public mandate is also notable: 66.4% of residents voted in favour of hosting the Olympic and Paralympic Games in a referendum.What should Ahmedabad learn from Munich?Munich's strongest argument is that it may not need to build as much as its rivals. That is a direct challenge to Ahmedabad's model. India's plans involve a major programme of urban development and sports infrastructure around the city. Munich, by contrast, is presenting existing venues and legacy reuse as competitive advantages.For Ahmedabad, the lesson is to explain not just how much infrastructure will be developed, but also how much can be reused, how much it will cost to maintain and what the city will gain in return. A compelling Olympic proposal must be an urban development plan as well as a sports master plan.South AfricaSouth Africa wants to bring the Summer Olympics to Africa for the first time. Its case combines the symbolic significance of being the first African host with the country's existing experience of delivering major international sporting events.South Africa has never hosted an Olympic Games. Its major-event record includes the 1995 Rugby World Cup and the 2010 FIFA World Cup.The latter is especially relevant because it demonstrated the country's ability to stage a global event across multiple venues and cities. It also offers an example of how a major tournament can be used to develop or upgrade infrastructure.The country has explored hosting the Olympics for several years, with the government approving its entry into the IOC's Continuous Dialogue process for a potential 2036 or 2040 Games.What is South Africa's 2036 project?The proposal initially outlined by South African Olympic leadership is a multi-city model involving Cape Town, Johannesburg and Durban.The logic is to distribute venues and responsibilities across existing urban centres rather than force the entire event into one city. It draws inspiration from the use of multiple locations at Paris 2024 and aims to make greater use of existing facilities.The three cities offer different strengths:- Cape Town: A globally recognisable setting and a proposed centre of the national project.- Johannesburg: Major-event experience and established sporting infrastructure, including FNB Stadium.- Durban: Existing major sports facilities, including Moses Mabhida Stadium.The final configuration remains subject to development. South African officials have also indicated that a preferred host city would need to be selected as the project progresses.What should Ahmedabad learn from South Africa?South Africa and India are both trying to make a larger historical argument through the Olympics. For South Africa, success would mean hosting the first Summer Olympics on African soil. For India, it would mean hosting the country's first Olympic Games and taking a major step towards its ambition of becoming a global sporting power.Both can argue that hosting would expand participation and create a wider sporting legacy. Both also need to show that their national ambitions are backed by credible funding, reliable governance and realistic plans for coordinating the host locations.The key distinction is that South Africa's project is explicitly designed to spread the Games across multiple cities. India's proposal is centred on Ahmedabad, even though the benefits of hosting would be national.TürkiyeIstanbul is trying to turn repeated Olympic disappointment into a stronger, more mature proposal, using existing infrastructure and upcoming international events to demonstrate readiness. Istanbul has made five previous unsuccessful attempts to host the Summer Olympics: 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012 and 2020.The 2020 campaign is especially relevant because Istanbul reached the final vote, finishing behind Tokyo. The city therefore has experience of an Olympic campaign at the highest level but has yet to convince the IOC to award it the Games.Türkiye's current bid process has been underway for several years. The Turkish National Olympic Committee (TMOK) says it formally backed Istanbul's candidacy in April 2024 and entered the IOC's Continuous Dialogue process.What is Türkiye's 2036 project?Istanbul's proposal combines existing venues and infrastructure with a wider national effort to demonstrate its ability to organise major competitions.The city's Olympic authorities, the Ministry of Youth and Sports, Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality and the Turkish Paralympic Committee have been involved in presenting the project's vision to the IOC. Their work has addressed the expected impact of the Games, the legacy plan and the relationship between the Olympic project and Istanbul's urban development objectives.The most important practical milestone is the 2027 European Games, which Türkiye intends to use as a rehearsal for its Olympic ambition.TMOK has described the event as a live rehearsal and a test of confidence. The intention is to demonstrate venue readiness, transport and logistics, operational capacity and the ability to work with international sporting bodies before the IOC makes its decision on the 2036 Games.Türkiye's government has also pointed to its experience of hosting major sporting competitions, ongoing investment in swimming facilities and the availability of an Olympic Village. Those claims will need to be assessed alongside the complete competition-venue plan and the wider logistics of the proposed Games.What should Ahmedabad learn from Türkiye?Istanbul's advantage is that it has repeatedly pursued the Olympics and understands the demands of the bidding process. However, its history also demonstrates that persistence and a strong city identity do not guarantee success.The 2027 European Games offer a useful parallel with Ahmedabad's role in the 2030 Commonwealth Games. Both cities have a major multisport event that can serve as evidence of their ability to host something larger.For Ahmedabad, the critical question will be whether the Commonwealth Games become a genuine test of operational readiness and long-term planning, rather than simply a milestone on the way to an Olympic bid.HungaryHungary is exploring a bid to host the 2036 Olympic and Paralympic Games in Budapest, with a vision centred on existing and temporary venues rather than the construction of new permanent stadiums. The proposed model envisages at least 80% of events taking place in Hungary, with the possibility of sharing venues with neighbouring countries.Budapest has pursued Olympic hosting ambitions for the 1916, 1920, 1936 and 1960 Games, but none resulted in the city being awarded the event. Its most recent campaign was for the 2024 Olympics, but it was withdrawn in February 2017 after the Momentum Movement gathered approximately 266,000 signatures demanding a referendum on the proposal.Since then, Hungary has hosted several major international sporting events, including the 2017 and 2022 World Aquatics Championships and the 2023 World Athletics Championships. These events have strengthened the country's experience in organising international competitions, although an Olympic bid would still require broad political consensus and firm financial guarantees.What is Hungary's 2036 project?The proposed Games would draw on Hungary's existing sporting infrastructure, including Puskás Aréna, the National Athletics Centre, MVM Dome and Duna Aréna. Where suitable facilities are unavailable, organisers could consider temporary venues or explore sharing facilities with other countries. Preliminary discussions have included possible venues in Vienna, Bratislava, Košice, Brno, Ljubljana, Zagreb, Belgrade and Cluj-Napoca, although no final agreements have been reached.What should Ahmedabad learn from Hungary?Hungary's proposition is about hosting the Olympics with less new permanent construction, while Ahmedabad's is about using the Olympics to accelerate sporting and urban development.- Venues: Hungary prioritises existing and temporary facilities, potentially supplemented by venues across Central Europe. Ahmedabad's plans centre on a proposed sports enclave and wider infrastructure development.- Legacy: Hungary emphasises avoiding underused stadiums and investing in infrastructure that Budapest already needs. Ahmedabad frames the Games as a catalyst for wider participation and India's sporting ambitions.- Experience: Hungary has recently staged major international championships. Ahmedabad's 2030 Commonwealth Games offer an opportunity to demonstrate its ability to deliver a multisport event.- Main obstacle: Hungary needs political agreement and a workable cross-border model. Ahmedabad needs to demonstrate that its infrastructure plans, funding, governance and operational capabilities can meet Olympic requirements.- The key contrast: Hungary asks whether the Olympics can be staged with minimal new permanent stadium construction. Ahmedabad asks whether the Olympics can justify and accelerate a major programme of development.What is Ahmedabad's plan for the 2036 Games?India's campaign is framed around the vision "Rising Together" and the idea that hosting the Games could transform the country's sporting ecosystem, rather than merely stage a fortnight of competition. The Indian Olympic Association (IOA) has described the ambition as an opportunity to increase participation, strengthen communities and create opportunities through sport.IOA CEO Raghuram Iyer has also made the ambition explicit: India wants to become a sporting superpower, with the longer-term goal of entering the world's top five or top 10 sporting nations.India's own project- Sports City: Plans associated with the Commonwealth Games include 11 sports complexes and complementary facilities such as gyms, swimming pools and training spaces.- Municipal investment: Ahmedabad's draft municipal budget for 2026-27 earmarked ₹17,018 crore for development, including mobility, sustainability and urban development.- 2030 Commonwealth Games: These provide a nearer-term opportunity to test venue delivery and event operations.- 2038 Asian Games: India has also pursued Ahmedabad as a possible host, potentially creating a sequence of major multisport events leading towards the Olympic ambition.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘I know he is watching from above’: Lalremsiami’s gold-sealing goal, emotional tribute to late father and a Mizo heroine’s homecoming
articles.summary: KOLKATA: Lalremsiami Hmarzote’s thoughts drifted to her late father as thousands lined the streets of Mizoram to celebrate India’s historic women’s hockey
articles.body: KOLKATA: Lalremsiami Hmarzote’s thoughts drifted to her late father as thousands lined the streets of Mizoram to celebrate India’s historic women’s hockey gold medal at the Asian Games.“I know he would be proud of me and is watching me from heaven,” the forward told TOI, reflecting on a campaign that saw her score seven goals, including the lone strike in the final against China, as India ended a 44-year wait for Asian Games gold and sealed qualification for the Los Angeles Olympics.The reception back home was overwhelming for the Mizo star, who returned to a heroine’s welcome after playing a key role in India’s triumphant run.“The whole of Mizoram celebrated with us. The chief minister, sports minister and so many people came out to welcome us. When we arrived at the airport, there was a grand reception and everyone made us feel very special,” Lalremsiami said.The roadshow through her hometown of Kolasib, 85km north of the state capital, Aizawl, lined with cheering crowds and children eager to catch a glimpse of their sporting hero, left a deep impression on her. “Many children and young people came up to meet me and told me they were inspired by what we had achieved. That made me very happy because if our success can motivate someone to take up sports, then it means a lot,” she said.While the celebrations were memorable, the Asian Games final remains the defining moment of her career, which began with her India debut in 2017. The occasion carried added significance as it was her 200th international match, and she admitted the pressure before the game was unlike anything she had experienced.“I was extremely nervous. It was my 200th match, it was the final, and we knew that if we won, we would make history after 44 years and qualify for the LA Olympics,” she said.“I prayed before the match and asked God to help me. Once the game started, I was able to play freely. To score the goal and help my team and my country win the gold medal was simply amazing. It is a moment I will never forget.”While many people have supported her journey, much of her motivation, she says, came from her father, who backed her hockey dreams from the very beginning before passing away in 2019.“My father played a very important role in my career and in my life. He was the one who inspired me and supported me when I was young and just starting hockey. He always believed in me and stood by me every step of the way,” she said. “He is not with us anymore, but the things he told me are still alive inside me. I know he would be proud of me today.”Lalremsiami also credited the team’s unity, coach Sjoerd Marijne and the support staff for a remarkable run this year that included World Cup qualification, Nations Cup success, a fifth-place finish at the World Cup and Asian Games gold.“We have gone through a lot of struggles over the years. Our unity within the group has been one of our biggest strengths. Success is not just about the players on the field. It is about the whole team working together,” she said.The 26-year-old was also part of the Indian side that registered the country’s best Women’s World Cup finish in 52 years. But the focus has already shifted to the Los Angeles Olympics, now less than two years away, and the forward believes India must continue to improve despite becoming Asian champions.“We have one dream now. We want to do well at the World Cup and win an Olympic medal. We know it will be very challenging, but we are ready for it,” she said.Even as she dreams of an Olympic podium finish, Lalremsiami hopes to see more girls from Mizoram take up the sport that has given her everything. While the challenges remain, she urged youngsters not to let those limitations hold them back.“My message to young girls is simple: keep dreaming and keep believing in yourselves. There is a lot of talent in Mizoram. I hope we get more grounds, more academies and better facilities in the future so that more children get the opportunity to play hockey and follow their dreams.”Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games CEO Cindy Hook to step down
articles.summary: Cindy Hook, the chief executive officer of the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games organising committee, will step down at the end of her four-year
articles.body: Cindy Hook, the chief executive officer of the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games organising committee, will step down at the end of her four-year contract later this year. The organisers announced her decision on Tuesday, a week after unveiling the official emblems for the Games.Hook, who was appointed in December 2022, said she was proud of the work done to build the organisation and prepare for the event. She believes the committee is now ready for new leadership as preparations move forward.“As CEO, I am proud to have built the organization from the ground up, set the Games Vision and Games Plan, designed and executed a clear strategy, created the brand narrative and launched incredible emblems, and driven early market momentum,” Hook said, as quoted by news agency AP, in the statement. “The foundations for success have been well laid. This is the right time to hand over to a new CEO."The organisers said the search for her replacement would begin immediately to ensure a smooth change in leadership as the project moves from early planning to operational work and event delivery.Organisers praise Hook's contributionBrisbane 2032 president Andrew Liveris praised Hook for building the committee from a small startup into an established organisation.“Cindy has been an exceptional leader whose passion, drive and strategic intellect has set Brisbane 2032 up for success,” Liveris said.He also credited her with building a strong team and putting proper financial management and governance systems in place.Australian Olympic Committee president Ian Chesterman said Hook had helped lay the groundwork for a successful Games and a lasting legacy for Australia.“Her leadership has laid strong foundations for the successful delivery of the Games in 2032,” Chesterman said.Brisbane 2032 board director Rebecca Frizelle also praised Hook's leadership and commitment.Brisbane prepares for historic GamesBrisbane was awarded the 2032 Olympics in July 2021 and will become the third Australian city to host the Summer Games, after Melbourne in 1956 and Sydney in 2000.Hook previously served as CEO of Deloitte Asia Pacific while based in Singapore before taking charge of the Brisbane organising committee. Her departure comes as preparations enter a new phase, with organisers now looking for a successor to lead the next stages of planning and delivery.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Alejandro Blanco: "No entiendo el olimpismo del futuro sin el pádel"
articles.standfirst: El presidente del COE elogió la realidad del deporte de la pala en la Asamblea General de la FIP a la que acudieron 115 federaciones nacionales de todo el mundo.
articles.summary: El presidente del COE elogió la realidad del deporte de la pala en la Asamblea General de la FIP a la que acudieron 115 federaciones nacionales de todo el mundo.
articles.body: el pádel continúa dando pasos para cumplir el gran sueño olímpico y el último gesto público, aunque simbólico, refuerza su candidatura como deporte participante en las próximas ediciones de los Juegos Olímpicos. Durante la celebración de la Asamblea General de la Federación Internacional de Pádel (FIP) celebrada en Madrid este lunes, Alejandro Blanco, presidente del Comité Olímpico Español (COE), analizaría el crecimiento del deporte de la pala. "Lo digo desde hace mucho tiempo: el pádel tiene un papel importante que desempeñar en el futuro del deporte y no entendería el futuro del movimiento olímpico sin que formase parte de él”, explicaba Blanco ante un abarrotado salón de actos del COE. Opciones que pasan, según voces autorizadas, por mantener la vista puesta en Brisbane 2032 y cuyas claves se cimentan en tres pilares. “De cara al futuro del movimiento olímpico, la participación, el alcance internacional y el impacto de un deporte en la sociedad serán fundamentales. El pádel cuenta con argumentos sólidos en los tres ámbitos", continuó. Un discurso en el que Blanco elogiaría la labor de Luigi Carraro, presidente de la FIP y máximo exponente del camino olímpico del pádel, asegurando "que bajo el liderazgo de mi gran amigo Luigi Carraro y su equipo, creo que lo mejor está por llegar". La trigesimosexta edición de la Asamblea FIP serviría para debatir las diferentes propuestas sobre la mesa y que daría la bienvenida a nuevos miembros en territorios donde el pádel empieza a dar sus primeros pasos. Según han comunicado desde el propio ente federativo, tras la incorporación de los nuevos socios el pádel cuenta ya con 115 federaciones nacionales que, en palabras del propio Carraro, "refleja una comunidad mundial del pádel unida por una visión compartida y un espíritu de cooperación". Un movimiento de expansión internacional que mantiene al pádel como uno de los deportes de mayor crecimiento a nivel global y que sigue conquistando territorios en los cinco continentes, requisito indispensable (entre otros) para cumplir con la carta olímpica, la llave de acceso a los Juegos Olímpicos.

articles.title: El 'Capitán América' vuelve a la Asobal
articles.standfirst: El estadounidense Drew Dolin, que jugó dos temporadas en el Ademar León, ficha por el Atlético Valladolid
articles.summary: El estadounidense Drew Dolin, que jugó dos temporadas en el Ademar León, ficha por el Atlético Valladolid
articles.body: Andrew Donlin regresa al balonmano español. El central estadounidense, de 34 años y 2,02 metros, se incorpora a la disciplina del Atlético Valladolid para reforzar la defensa después de la marcha del egipcio Gedo. Donlin, militar profesional, ya jugó en la Asobal. Llegó al Ademar León en la temporada 2019-20 tras cruzarse con Manolo Cadenas, por entonces seleccionador argentino, en los Juegos Panamericanos de Lima en 2019. Cambió el Bayer Dormagen alemán por jugar en España. Prolongó su presencia por otra temporada tras renovar su acuerdo con el ejército norteamericano para continuar en el 'Programa de Atletas de Clase Mundial'. "Estoy muy agradecido por esta oportunidad de jugar con el Atlético Valladolid y también para empezar a trabajar con el equipo. Es un club con mucha historia y el equipo ha tenido un inicio increíble de la temporada. Quiero aprender de David Pisonero y tengo mucha ilusión de estar en Valladolid para competir a alto nivel en una temporada larga y dura. Personalmente quiero crecer deportivamente y también ayudar al equipo en lo que pueda", comenta Donlin que mantiene vivo el objetivo de ser olímpico en su país en los Juegos de Los Ángeles 2028. Tras su experiencia en nuestro país, volvió a la liga de Estados Unidos. Jugó cuatro temporadas en el San Francisco CalHeat y este pasado curso en Los Ángeles HC. Ha sido internacional su b21, y absoluto con Estados Unidos desde 2016. Jugó los Mundiales de 2023 y 2025. No pudo hacer lo propio en 2021 ya que el COVID provocó que la selección estadounidense no jugará el torneo. "Donlin cumple muchas de las premisas que buscábamos. Lo primero un perfil meramente defensivo y él es un especialista en este tema. Su predisposición total de estar aquí es una de las garantías que tenemos y lo que ha precipitado las cosas. Es un jugador físicamente muy potente, agresivo, muy disciplinado y que defensivamente se va a acoplar rápido al sistema del equipo ayudando y sumando en la rotación", comentó Pisonero, entrenador del Valladolid.

articles.title: Swansong for four Indian hockey seniors at Asian Champions Trophy
articles.summary: For some of India’s Olympic medallists, the Asian Champions Trophy could be one last march in national colours.
articles.body: For some of India’s Olympic medallists, the Asian Champions Trophy could be one last march in national colours. With international hockey returning to Punjab after 17 years, the tournament later this month is set to usher in a change of guard, with at least four senior players facing the exit as India begin rebuilding for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.India, who clinched the Asian Games gold in Japan to secure their Olympic berth, will continue to be led by Harmanpreet Singh. But the tournament, beginning in Jalandhar on Oct 27 and concluding in Mohali on Nov 5, will be the final assignment in India colours for Mandeep Singh, Jarmanpreet Singh, Amit Rohidas and Nilakanta Sharma, according to sources.All four, who are in their 30s, have been part of India’s Olympic bronze medal-winning campaigns over the previous two editions. Hockey India selection committee chairman RP Singh declined to name the players but confirmed that at least half a dozen could feature in their final matches for India at the ACT.“It is time to get fresh legs into the team. I cannot name the players, but they have been informed about the situation. We believe they deserve an honourable exit. With Punjab hosting an international tournament after nearly two decades, it is only fitting that some of them sign off on home turf,” Singh told TOI.“With the Olympics less than two years away, it gives the coaching staff enough time to groom them,” he added. Singh also said a team comprising the remaining senior players and fresh faces would tour New Zealand in Nov, giving chief coach Craig Fulton an opportunity to assess young talent in overseas conditions. India are the defending champions of ACT.The squad:Goalkeepers: Suraj Karkera; Krishan Pathak; Defenders: Sanjay, Harmanpreet Singh (c), Amit Rohidas, Jugraj Singh, Jarmanpreet Singh, Amandeep Lakra; Midfielders: Rajinder Singh, Aditya Lalage, Nilakanta Sharma, Hardik Singh, Manpreet Singh; Forwards: Shilanand Lakra, Abhishek, Sukhjeet Singh, Dilpreet Singh, Mandeep Singh.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: From barefoot runs to Olympic podiums: India’s daughters win medals, but why does our sports policy fail them?
articles.summary: India’s sporting daughters are defeating poverty, hunger, gender discrimination and the absence of basic facilities to win medals at national and
articles.body: India’s sporting daughters are defeating poverty, hunger, gender discrimination and the absence of basic facilities to win medals at national and international competitions. Their extraordinary journeys raise an uncomfortable question: why does the system celebrate champions after victory instead of identifying, supporting and nurturing them before they become champions? Himachal Pradesh, like the rest of India, needs a fundamental rethink of its sports policy.Imagine a young girl in a remote Himalayan village running barefoot to school, sprinting along mountain paths in torn shoes, and returning home to help her family before finding time to practise her favourite sport. There is no synthetic track, no modern gymnasium, no nutritionist and often no qualified coach. Her parents struggle to put two nutritious meals on the table. Yet, she dreams of representing India at the Olympics.Somewhere in rural India, a mother may be selling her goats, borrowing money or even parting with a piece of family land to finance her daughter’s sporting ambition. Elsewhere, a budding shooter depends on borrowed equipment, a boxer practises punches against sandbags hanging in a cowshed, and a wrestler trains in a makeshift village akhara, fighting opponents on soil rather than on professionally maintained mats.These are not merely stories of sporting determination. They expose the contradictions of a system that expects world-class performances from athletes who are frequently denied world-class opportunities.Why must a poor family make extraordinary sacrifices before the government recognises an extraordinary talent?Champions who challenged more than their opponentsIndia’s sporting history is rich with women who overcame adversity to reach the highest podiums.Haryana’s Sakshi Malik, raised in a society where women wrestlers had to challenge entrenched gender stereotypes, won an Olympic bronze medal at Rio 2016. Her achievement demonstrated that determination, sustained training and opportunity could overcome barriers that had long kept girls away from wrestling.Vinesh Phogat, from Haryana’s celebrated wrestling family, fought her way into the international elite despite social resistance and the formidable pressures of competitive sport. Her career also reminds us that athletes must navigate the institutions governing their sports, not merely defeat opponents on the mat.From Manipur, Mary Kom rose from a modest background to become a multiple-time world boxing champion and an Olympic bronze medallist at London 2012. Her journey challenged assumptions about women, motherhood, poverty and participation in a physically demanding sport.Lovlina Borgohain, from Assam, overcame financial and infrastructural constraints to become an international boxing star, winning an Olympic bronze medal at Tokyo 2020.Then there is Avani Lekhara, who won two gold medals at the Tokyo 2020 Paralympics, demonstrating extraordinary skill and resilience in shooting. Her achievements underline the importance of accessible training, specialised equipment and sustained institutional support.The journeys of Salima Tete and Nikki Pradhan, from Jharkhand, also illustrate how players from relatively disadvantaged regions can rise through the ranks of Indian women’s hockey and compete on the international stage.These athletes did not face identical circumstances. Nor should their individual journeys be reduced to a single narrative of poverty. Yet, their achievements share an important lesson: India’s sporting talent is distributed far more widely than its quality sporting infrastructure.The failure of medal-first mindsetOur sports administration often appears most enthusiastic after an athlete has won a medal. Cash awards, government jobs, felicitations and headlines follow success. But who pays for years of uncertain training, expensive equipment, travel, coaching and nutrition before that moment?For a poor family, the cost of a shooting rifle, boxing gear, wrestling equipment or repeated journeys to a training centre can be prohibitive. In remote Himalayan settlements, distance, difficult terrain and inadequate transport add another layer of disadvantage.A child without access to a trained coach may never discover her potential. A talented girl may abandon sport because her family cannot afford nutritious food or safe accommodation. Another may leave because social prejudice discourages her from travelling away from home.These are lost medals that never appear in official statistics.The fundamental weakness is not necessarily the absence of sports policies or schemes. It is the failure to ensure that opportunities reach talented children early, consistently and equitably.Himachal Pradesh needs a grassroots sporting revolutionFor Himachal Pradesh, this challenge is particularly significant. Scattered settlements, mountainous terrain and long distances make centralised sports facilities insufficient. A policy designed around district headquarters and established academies cannot adequately serve children in remote villages.The state needs a decentralised, village-first approach. Seema’s bronze medal at the recent Asian Games in Japan, and her hunger for a medal at the next Olympics, show how she and her family from a remote village in Chamba have suffered and overcome adversity. She is not alone. There are many Seemas, Ritu Negis and Bhavna Thakurs who have the talent, grit and potential to reach the pinnacle of sport. But what needs to be done?First, schools, panchayats and local sports clubs should conduct regular talent-identification programmes, with special outreach to girls and economically disadvantaged children.Second, promising athletes must receive support before winning medals: nutritious meals, equipment, coaching, travel assistance, scholarships and access to suitable training facilities. Selection should consider demonstrated potential, commitment, financial need and training requirements, rather than previous medals alone.Third, safe hostels, female coaches, reliable transport, clean sanitation facilities and effective grievance-redressal mechanisms must become integral to women’s sports development.Fourth, Himachal should prioritise functional village-level training facilities, qualified coaches and regular competitions over an excessive emphasis on expensive infrastructure that remains underutilised. Remote and tribal regions need programmes adapted to their geography and local sporting traditions.Finally, sports budgets must be transparent. The government should publish information on expenditure reaching grassroots athletes, the distribution of facilities, the availability of coaches and the progress of supported players. Independent evaluations should establish whether public investment is actually expanding access and improving performance.These reforms should complement national initiatives, including Khelo India, through measurable outcomes rather than announcements alone.Invest in potential, not just podiumsIndia’s daughters have demonstrated that world-class sporting ability does not belong exclusively to metropolitan cities, affluent families or elite academies. It can emerge from a village akhara, a modest school playground or a makeshift training space.But for every Mary Kom, Sakshi Malik, Lovlina Borgohain or Avani Lekhara who reaches the international stage, how many potentially gifted girls never get the opportunity to begin?We celebrate the champion who raises the tricolour, yet rarely ask whether the next champion has proper shoes, adequate food, a qualified coach or money to travel to the next competition.The success of a sports policy must not be measured only by the medals won. It must also be measured by how many talented children are discovered, supported and given a fair chance to compete.Governments must honour their champions, but their greater responsibility is to identify tomorrow’s champions before poverty, distance, gender discrimination and inadequate facilities extinguish their dreams.India’s next Olympic medallist may be running barefoot on a village road today.The question is not whether she has the talent to win. The question is whether our sports policy will give her the opportunity to try.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: Usain Bolt comparisons a 'privilege', says South Africa's Sinesipho Dambile
articles.summary: South African sprinter Sinesipho Dambile says comparisons with Usain Bolt are a “privilege” as he targets World Championship and Olympic glory after a breakout season.
articles.body:
Commonwealth 200m champion Sinesipho Dambile says it is a "privilege" to be compared with Jamaican great Usain Bolt as he looks to establish himself among the world's leading sprinters.

The South African has enjoyed a breakthrough season, producing a string of impressive performances and underlining his credentials as one of Africa's emerging track stars.

Speaking to the Warm Up Track podcast, the 24-year-old revealed that he "enjoys the pressure" that comes with being mentioned alongside the fastest man in history.

"Pressure is a privilege," he said. "I love it because that's where I excel."

Dambile recalls meeting the eight-time Olympic champion at the 2025 World Athletics Championships in Tokyo, where the Jamaican offered him some advice.

"For Bolt, charisma naturally goes to him. Being able to meet him in person last year in Tokyo, he said: 'Please make sure you enjoy this thing'.

"That, until this day, still stuck with me."

Victory at last year's South African national championships secured Dambile's place in Tokyo, where he finished eighth in the 200m final, having set a new personal best of 19.97 seconds in the semi-finals.

That time was broken this season as Dambile accelerated his development.

June's Diamond League meeting in Doha saw him clock 19.74 seconds - the fourth-fastest time recorded by any athlete in 2026.

He went on to finish second behind the USA's Kenny Bednarek, but ahead of Botswana's 2024 Olympic champion Letsile Tebogo, in last month's Diamond League final in Brussels, while he was fourth in the inaugural Ultimate Championships.

However, the year's high point was undoubtedly the Commonwealth gold medal won in Birmingham in July, a result which made him the first South African to win the event.

While it is clear the 200m remains Dambile's principal event, he is "mentally willing to put in the work" to mimic Bolt, who likewise began his career specialising in the longer distance before going on to also dominate the 100m.

"He (Bolt) paved the way," Dambile said.

"I spoke to my team a couple of times and I was like, 'I want you guys to count me in on the 100m'.

"I want to do both. I know I'm going to be successful."

How Kenya won its bid for 2029 World Athletics Championships

A relaxed character, Dambile insists he will follow Bolt's advice to enjoy his time on the track, promising that fans will "get more of my personality" in future.

"I've never been a loud person, trying to bring attention to me," he said, contrasting his approach to the brash showmanship of Olympic 100m champion Noah Lyles.

"I'm always smiling out there, I'm always looking at the crowd, looking at the kids, and that's just me.

"I just want to go out there and do my thing, to make sure that everybody enjoys the show."

Dambile's success has coincided with a growing sense of belief within South African sprinting.

He was part of the quartet that won 4x100m gold at the World Relays in Guangzhou last year, running alongside team-mates Bayanda Walaza, Bradley Nkoana and Akani Simbine.

"We go as a squad, so we have that little bit of energy," Dambile said when explaining how the group's camaraderie has played an important role in their success.

"We pump each other up because we're going for the one thing - doing it for our country.

"The biggest sport in our country is rugby, so you get the Springboks going there winning the World Cup and we wanted to have the same feeling."

The influence of the experienced Simbine has been crucial.

The 2018 Commonwealth 100m champion finally landed an Olympic medal at Paris 2024, picking up silver in the 4x100m relay, having agonisingly finished fourth in the individual 100m finals in both the French capital and at the 2020 Games in Tokyo.

"He's made all the finals. He's been there. He's been the guy. He's been one of the best sprinters in the world," said Dambile.

"So when someone like that from home can do it, we also start to believe that it's actually possible to do it."

How 'sub-10 king' Simbine shed his nearly man tag

Luxolo Adams talks mental fitness and 'arrogant faces'

Just like Simbine, Dambile is a product of the TuksSport team at the University of Pretoria, a breeding ground for South Africa's top talent, including fellow sprinter Gift Leotlela, who finished fourth in the 100m final at this year's Commonwealth Games, and 2025 world indoor 800m champion Prudence Sekgodiso.

"We all were scouted through different processes and we all ended up at the same school," said Dambile.

All four Pretoria alumni competed in Birmingham this year, but only Dambile came away with a Commonwealth medal.

"It was so much relief because what I did was not just a small thing," he explained.

"It was huge, especially for myself [and] the country of South Africa. My emotions were all over the place.

"I just pushed through everything and when I was in that moment, I knew I deserved it because of the amount of work I've put in."

A double medallist at the 2021 Under-20 World Championships in Nairobi, Dambile's progression from promising junior to established senior athlete has not, however, been straightforward, with injury curtailing much of his 2024 season.

"It's easier to recognise me in the country now with me winning the Commonwealth," he explained.

"A bit of fame now - you can see people when they talk about you. It's like I've been experiencing beautiful things happening."

Things could get even better with plans already being made for next year's World Championships in Beijing and the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.

"We've already set up a map towards that," he said.

"We definitely know how important it's going to be over the next two years.

"I want to be the best 200m athlete the sport has ever seen.

"I need to make sure that I have the World Championship [and] Olympic title. I want to do things that have never been done in my country."

articles.title: 17-year wait ends: Asian Champions Trophy brings international hockey back to Punjab after long gap
articles.summary: International hockey will return to Punjab after 17 years when India host the men's Asian Champions Trophy for the second time, with Jalandhar and Mohali
articles.body: International hockey will return to Punjab after 17 years when India host the men's Asian Champions Trophy for the second time, with Jalandhar and Mohali set to stage the tournament from October 27 to November 2.The last international hockey tournament held in the state was the 2009 Punjab Gold Cup.Hockey has a special place in Punjab, which has played a major role in shaping Indian hockey through its villages, academies and generations of players who have represented the country at the highest level.The upcoming tournament will feature six teams — hosts India, Malaysia, South Korea, China, Japan and Bangladesh — competing for the title.India, the reigning Asian Games champions, are the most successful team in the tournament's history, having won the title five times in 2011, 2016, 2018 (joint winners), 2023 and 2024.Punjab's contribution to Indian hockey spans generations, from former greats Udham Singh and Balbir Singh Sr to current players Manpreet Singh and Harmanpreet Singh.India captain Harmanpreet, who led the team to gold medals at two successive Asian Games, said the tournament would be special for the players from Punjab, who will get the opportunity to represent the country on home soil."It's going to be a special occasion for the entire team, especially for the players who belong to Punjab because it's the first time that we will be wearing India jersey at an international tournament in Punjab," Harmanpreet Singh, the first captain to lead India to successive Asian Games gold medal triumphs, said in a Hockey India release."My entire family is expected to be at the stadium watching me play an international match together from the venue for the first time, including my father who has never seen me play for the country while sitting inside the stadium."The Olympian Surjit Singh Hockey Stadium at Burlton Park in Jalandhar will host the opening ceremony and league-stage matches from October 27 to November 2. The stadium is named after Surjit Singh, the celebrated defender who was part of India's 1975 World Cup-winning team.The tournament will then move to the Olympian Balbir Singh Senior International Hockey Stadium in Mohali, which will host the semifinals and medal matches on November 4 and 5.All six teams will face each other once in the league stage, with the top four advancing to the semifinals.Defending champions India will begin their campaign against Bangladesh in Jalandhar on October 27.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Otra de 'indios' y 'vikingos': 10 km a toda velocidad en el derbi sobre el asfalto
articles.standfirst: Abel Resino y Antonio Adán, padrinos de los equipos del Atlético y el Real Madrid, dieron la salida en MARCA al ‘Derbi de las Aficiones Aliexpress Marcas+ Chuwi’ del 25 de octubre
articles.summary: Abel Resino y Antonio Adán, padrinos de los equipos del Atlético y el Real Madrid, dieron la salida en MARCA al ‘Derbi de las Aficiones Aliexpress Marcas+ Chuwi’ del 25 de octubre
articles.body: Apenas un mes después de que Atlético de Madrid y Real Madrid disputaran el primer derbi liguero de esta temporada, 10.000 corredores, cinco mil de cada equipo, se darán cita el próximo 25 de octubre en las calles de la capital en el ‘Derbi de las Aficiones Aliexpress Marcas+ Chuwi’, que se presentó este miércoles en MARCA. Será la decimosexta edición de este particular derbi en el asfalto, que se disputa sobre 10 kilómetros, con un recorrido que en los últimos años ha mejorado aún más en el primer tramo hasta convertirse en una de las pruebas más rápidas del calendario. Abel Resino y Antonio Adán, padrinos de los equipos de Atlético y Real Madrid, dieron el pistoletazo de salida a esta carrera, ya consolidada en el panorama nacional, que dominan los 'vikingos' en la serie histórica por 9-6. "Es una iniciativa genial porque más allá de la rivalidad que existe entre las dos aficiones es un día para disfrutarlo", aseguró Resino, leyenda del Atlético de Madrid, que recordó cómo eran los derbis futbolísticos cuando jugaba. "Para empezar, en los derbis de mi época no había VAR, lo cual era un tema difícil y complicado. Había mucha más rivalidad. Yo creo que en esa época el juego era más duro, había más choque". Por su parte, Antonio Adán, exjugador del Real Madrid, destacó que "esta carrera representa unos valores tremendos. Que en una ciudad como Madrid puedan convivir dos aficiones tan grandes y que se unan en esta prueba en un día de fiesta, es realmente fantástico". Aunque por el momento no disputará la prueba. "He estado en el mundo profesional del fútbol y ahora empezará otra etapa: pasar de ser futbolista a ser deportista en general, para poder dedicarme a otras actividades y de momento no me he iniciado en la carrera. Siempre me ha parecido algo realmente duro, sobre todo desde el punto de vista mental". Con un bagaje de 9-6 para los 'vikingos', los atletas que correrán por el Real Madrid buscan la 'Décima' victoria. "Estoy confiado en que el Madrid siga al frente", admitía Adán. "Pero lo más importante es que sea un día para la diversión, para compartir a pesar de la rivalidad". Sin embargo, Abel Resino confía en la remontada en este ‘Derbi de las Aficiones Aliexpress Marcas+ Chuwi’, que cuenta también con el patrocinio de Toyota Hersamotor, Cabify y Supermercados BM. "Hay que ir a por esa remontada 9-7 y en unos añitos estamos igualados".
